population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. Arithmetic: ever 29.0 − current 21.3 = 7.7 pp of adults used and are off now; about 14.0 pp have stopped at least once, ~45% of them (6.3 pp) restarted and are counted in the current 21.3 (7.7 + 6.3 = 14.0), so cycled = 6.3/29 ≈ 22% of ever-users. That fits the parent's 36–47% restart range, with one-year persistence up from ~35% to ~45% as out-of-pocket cost falls toward $0–49. Age weights (adult shares ~21/33/24/22%) give ~21.3% overall. The 65+ figure more than doubles (9→20) under Medicare's generic-first model; the 50–64 peak rises to 32%. Bottom-third use (18%) is held down by Medicaid churn under work requirements, non-expansion-state gaps (filled only partly by free provision at HRSA health centres from Jul 2028) and lower persistence. Top-third use (24%) includes the largest share of users without obesity: about 1 in 6 current users nationally have BMI <30 and take low-dose 'metabolic/longevity' or 'calm' protocols. Off-drug populations: ~7.7% of adults are former users, many regaining weight. Most adults with obesity in Texas, Florida and other non-expansion states who earn too much for free provision but lack employer coverage pay $39–49 cash or go without. Pediatric: ~0.8% of under-18s (mostly 12–17, about 3–4% of adolescents with obesity), still skewed to insured upper-income families. Adult obesity estimated at ~33.5% (from 36.4% in 2026).

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot (Jul 2026–Dec 2027) became a multi-year CMS Innovation Center metabolic-health model running through 2031. Branded drugs stay at ~$245 to Medicare with a $50 copay. Since Jul 2028 new starts go generic-first: generic semaglutide at ~$30–35 to Medicare and $0 copay. Medicaid: 41 states + DC cover obesity at federally negotiated rates, generic-first; coverage is interrupted by Medicaid work-requirement churn from 2027. HRSA free provision (Jul 2028): generic semaglutide pens at no cost for uninsured adults ≤250% FPL with obesity or BMI ≥27 plus a comorbidity, through federally qualified health centres; it matters most in non-expansion states. VA covers generic-first. Public programmes now pay for ~52% of US incretin fills.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide in ~160 countries. India $6–30/month across 60+ brands; China's domestic generics launched 2026–27 and China is now the dominant peptide API exporter; Canada CAD 60–95; Brazil and Mexico widespread. Tirzepatide is still under patent nearly everywhere, which makes it and the unapproved retatrutide the main counterfeit targets.
access.note: US generic semaglutide injection arrived through a licensed settlement (Jun 2028), not patent expiry: Viatris and two other filers sell under licence, and Novo sells an authorised generic at $49 (TrumpRx listing $49; cost-plus pharmacies $39). Branded Wegovy list was cut to $799, but almost no one pays brand for semaglutide now. Oral semaglutide brand ~$149–199. Foundayo starts at $149. Zepbound via LillyDirect $349–499. Retatrutide (approved Apr 2028) lists at $1,299, is sold direct at $699 and is covered by almost no plan. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 46%; most remaining plans cover generic semaglutide only. Gray market peaked in 2027, when Indian and Chinese vials sold for $15–40 against US cash prices of $245–350. Since the generic launch it has shifted to tirzepatide and 'research' retatrutide, plus non-prescription wellness buyers avoiding prescribers. CBP GLP-1 seizures in 2027 were ~6× the 2026 level. FDA finalised the 503B exclusion in 2027.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic brand; licensed and authorised generic semaglutide injection from Jun 2028)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro; no generic)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Jan 2027)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed, not FDA-labelled. ASAM's Mar 2028 guideline recommends GLP-1 RAs as an option for AUD in patients with obesity or type 2 diabetes and as a consideration in others; the VA adopted it. Novo's phase 3 AUD trial (oral semaglutide) began 2027 and reads out 2029–30
low-dose 'metabolic health' / longevity use by adults without obesity, mostly generic semaglutide via telehealth at $39–99/month including the visit
'calm/focus' protocols: low-dose semaglutide marketed for craving, impulsivity and 'food noise'
nicotine, gambling and compulsive-shopping reduction: observational evidence and small RCTs, no guideline
pediatric under-12 use off-label under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Applied product by product. CagriSema (under review in the parent) was approved Jan 2027 despite failing non-inferiority to tirzepatide; it holds a niche on tolerability and Novo contracting. Retatrutide's BLA was filed Feb 2027 and approved Apr 2028 (14 months after filing): 28.3% mean loss at 80 weeks, labelled for dysesthesia, with a postmarketing requirement on neuropsychiatric and ocular outcomes. Amycretin remains in phase 3 (no filing; readouts 2029), so it is not on the market. Survodutide's phase 3 read out in 2027 (~16%) with no US filing. The monthly/implant driver is realised as a filing only: Amgen filed the MariTide BLA in Sep 2028 under a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher, decision expected Q1 2029. It was 'in development' in the parent, so no monthly or implantable incretin is on the US market at end-2028, and none has launched abroad either. Weekly injection and daily oral remain the adherence choice. Muscle-preserving adjuncts (bimagrumab) are in phase 2b/3, not approved; amylin monotherapies are in phase 3. Global incretin revenue has grown in volume, but US price per patient has fallen sharply for semaglutide.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation; higher with retatrutide at escalation. Counterfeit over-concentration produced severe-vomiting ER presentations in 2027.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; more visible with retatrutide's larger losses.
No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs; absolute risk low; signal noise from counterfeit cases.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; litigation ongoing, multidistrict proceedings unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About 25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, depending on drug, age and training. Concern is now concentrated in Medicare beneficiaries starting under generic-first rules and in non-obese wellness users. Bone-density signal persists in observational data.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No class label. The CMS model recommends, but does not require, resistance-training and protein counselling; muscle-preserving adjuncts are not yet approved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA Sentinel analysis plus two large cohorts found a small but consistent excess risk (on the order of 1.5–2× relative risk on a low baseline; absolute risk remains rare). Risk appears higher in people with diabetes and sleep apnoea. Ophthalmology referrals for sudden painless vision loss now routinely ask about incretin use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class-wide Warnings and Precautions label for all GLP-1 receptor agonists including dual/triple agonists (Sep 2027), with a patient Medication Guide section on sudden vision loss. EMA upgraded from 'very rare' to a warning in 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in EMA, MHRA and systematic-review evidence; no new signal.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed from Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound labels (Jan 2026); removal stands.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still unquantified in RCTs. Two observational survey studies (2027) put self-reported 'muted enjoyment' at roughly 10–20% of users, dose-related, with heavy confounding. The same mechanism is now guideline-endorsed for AUD and sold commercially as 'calm'.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label. FTC warning letters (2028) to telehealth firms over unsubstantiated 'focus/calm' claims; FDA says the claims imply unapproved indications but has not acted against prescribers.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Majority regain within 1–2 years in trials; real-world figures still conflict. Medicaid churn is producing involuntary stop-start cycles at scale.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; still drives chronic-therapy framing by manufacturers and payers.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signals for B12, iron, vitamin D and protein insufficiency, highest in older adults and in food-insecure households on free generic product.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; HRSA programme guidance recommends dietary screening but does not fund it.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exists for semaglutide; there are still no cycling data and no adolescent data beyond ~4 years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals (Foundayo, CagriSema, retatrutide); a CMS model registry collecting cycling data from 2028.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2027 import and counterfeit wave was linked to 200+ ER visits and 4 deaths in the May 2027 FDA/CDC report, and to thousands of adverse-event reports overall: mis-concentrated multi-dose vials, endotoxin-contaminated 'research' tirzepatide, and fake pens with Indian and Chinese packaging. Since the Jun 2028 generic launch the harms have shifted to unapproved retatrutide and tirzepatide peptides.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised (2027); FDA import alert on named Chinese peptide suppliers; CBP seizures ~6× 2026; DOJ prosecutions of Telegram resellers. Personal importation not tolerated.

safety_ledger.effect: Use in people without obesity (wellness/longevity/'calm' dosing)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No trial population resembles it. Concerns are lean-mass loss at normal BMI, low intake, and NAION benefit–risk in people with little metabolic benefit to set against it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None beyond FTC claims enforcement; state medical boards in California and New York issued advisory opinions on off-label wellness prescribing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in phase 3 and in post-launch reports; mostly mild and transient, dose-related.

food_and_beverage.state: Households with at least one incretin user are ~33%. US salty-snack and confectionery volumes are down ~4–6% cumulatively since 2026, and carbonated soft drinks ~3%. Two large CPG makers divested snack brands to private equity, which runs them for cash. Protein, fibre and 'small-format' lines are the only growing grocery segments. Discount grocers report the shift arriving in lower-income zip codes after free provision began in mid-2028, a lag behind affluent stores.

alcohol.state: US spirits depletions are down for a third straight year and beer volume keeps declining. The ASAM endorsement gave the heavy-drinker decline a clinical channel, with VA and some Medicaid AUD programmes prescribing. Brewers and distillers cut capacity and shift to premium and non-alcoholic lines. On-premise bars in affluent neighbourhoods report lower per-head spend but stable visits.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat and check composition keeps changing: half-portions, protein plates and fewer desserts and second drinks. Casual-dining chains depending on value bundles and bottomless offers are closing units. Fine dining and 'tasting menu' formats hold, selling occasion rather than volume.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are contracting further, with store closures and one restructuring. Mainstream brands extend petite and athletic lines. Tailoring and alteration demand has risen in metro areas, as has demand for fitted, arm-showing athleisure that signals muscle.

fitness.state: Strength-training studios, DEXA body-composition clinics and personal training are growing, concentrated in high-income metros. Budget gyms are flat. 'Lean-mass coaching' is a premium add-on for telehealth weight programmes. Medicare Advantage plans add resistance-training benefits as a marketing differentiator.

insurance.state: Commercial plans have retreated to generic-only or no coverage. Commercial pharmacy trend for incretins is falling for the first time since 2021 as members switch to $39–49 generic or public programmes. Medicare spending rose sharply in 2027 at $245 per branded month, prompting the generic-first switch in Jul 2028. Prior authorisation now mostly gates branded and next-generation drugs.

pharma.state: Global volume is still growing fast, but US semaglutide revenue per patient has collapsed. Novo traded the licence settlement and authorised generic for volume, tariff relief and Medicare position, and its margins and share price have fallen. Lilly leads on tirzepatide, Foundayo and retatrutide at premium prices. Indian and Chinese generic makers and API suppliers are the growth story outside the US. Amgen's MariTide is under review.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Weight loss itself has stopped signalling money: a free generic pen produces it. What the body signals now is how the weight was lost. Among Austin and Dallas tech and finance professionals, visible arm and shoulder muscle and DEXA lean-mass percentages, shown on phones, are the status marker. Among home health aides and warehouse workers in Houston, 'clinic thin' names a smaller but soft body, the result of free generic semaglutide without training or protein, and it is not meant kindly.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Price is no longer the gate for thinness; what money buys is the next-generation drug (retatrutide at $699 cash), coaching, protein and time to train. Bodies that cycle, losing on Medicaid and regaining when coverage lapses over work-requirement paperwork, are concentrated in the bottom income third. In Dallas's Park Cities private schools, adolescent prescribing by concierge paediatricians runs well ahead of the county clinics a few miles south.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: In GLP-1-heavy offices, shared meals shrink to coffee and a protein plate. In San Antonio and Houston Latino families, holiday tables are now negotiated: older relatives on Medicare generic eat little, and the cook's labour goes partly uneaten, a quiet source of friction reported by church food ministries. Protein shakes have become a breakfast habit among Medicare-age users following clinic handouts.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: On Miami dating apps 'on sema', 'on reta' and 'off, maintaining' appear in profiles as routinely as height. Some users read 'reta' as money and 'sema' as a clinic. Couples therapists in Denver describe 'desire discrepancy' intakes in which one partner is on a calm protocol. All anecdotal; unquantified.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dial rather than a self. In affluent circles, wanting something strongly, whether food, a second drink or the phone, is increasingly described as a symptom and dosed accordingly. In recovery communities in Columbus and Boston, the AUD endorsement has split meetings between people who see the drug as help and people who see it as skipping the work.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Still not measured in RCTs. Observational self-report puts 'muted enjoyment' at roughly 10–20% of users, dose-dependent and confounded. Telehealth firms now sell the effect at low doses (0.25–0.5 mg generic semaglutide) under brand names built on calm, quiet and focus; they report their own 'craving score' outcomes, which no regulator has validated.
interior_life.framing: In clinical settings: treatment (AUD, guideline-endorsed). In telehealth marketing: feature, 'freedom from craving'. In patient forums and the press: side effect. Among critics: character change. All four framings coexist, and the same 0.5 mg pen is all four depending on who prescribes it and why.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Calm protocols are popular among Chicago options traders, Phoenix call-centre team leads and enterprise sales floors, pitched as fewer impulse trades, less snacking and less doomscrolling. Managers report steadier output and less after-work drinking at client events. Some workers report losing the edge that made them good at closing. No employer mandates or pays for calm protocols; a few offer them through wellness stipends, which brushes against FTC scrutiny.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Nashville songwriters and Brooklyn DJs argue publicly about whether the drug flattens the work; several working musicians describe quitting it before tours. Bars in Austin and Brooklyn report quieter nights and lower spend with stable attendance. Sports-betting operators in Ohio and New Jersey flag lower deposit volatility among some high-value customers. Sour, spicy and extreme-flavour products keep selling to users seeking a felt reward.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Clinician and therapist anecdotes describe reduced libido and a 'pleasant distance' in some users, and better relationships in partners of users who stopped drinking heavily. The calm protocols have created a category of couples where one partner chose to want less.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The HRSA free-provision programme is attacked from two sides. Some progressive organisers and MAHA-aligned commentators call it 'sedating the poor with a free pen'; HHS defends it as obesity care. Ohio and New Jersey legislators have proposed funding GLP-1 pilots for gambling disorder. No measurable effect on voter mobilisation, but 'craving policy' has entered campaign vocabulary in health-heavy states.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access, price-focused and enforcement-heavy on supply. The administration claims the licensed generic and the $49 authorised generic as a price win. FDA moves next-generation drugs quickly (priority vouchers) while running import alerts, CBP seizure surges and prosecutions against counterfeit and research-peptide channels. It added the NAION class warning in 2027 and has not acted on 'calm' marketing beyond FTC letters.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy: since Jul 2028 the HRSA programme provides free generic semaglutide through FQHCs to uninsured adults ≤250% FPL who meet clinical criteria, funded at ~$3B/year. Medicare generic-first at $0 copay; Medicaid in 41 states + DC. No mandate for anyone.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Public coverage is conditioned on clinical criteria and, for Medicaid expansion adults, on work-requirement compliance. That produces lapses and involuntary cycling. The CMS model registry tracks fills, weights and discontinuation, an unprecedented longitudinal dataset. Some states require nutrition-visit attendance for renewal. No adherence surveillance beyond pharmacy fill data.
state.workforce_or_military: DoD issued accession guidance (2027) allowing applicants who reached body-composition standards on GLP-1s to enlist after a period of stable off-drug weight; recruiters informally steer overweight applicants to civilian prescribers. TRICARE covers generic semaglutide for dependants and retirees. No in-service mandate.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: China is the dominant peptide API supplier, and India the dominant finished-generic exporter, for most of the world and for the 2027 US gray market. The US licensed generic relies partly on Indian finished-dose manufacturing under FDA inspection. Tariff threats on pharmaceutical imports were traded for Novo's settlement and US fill-finish investment. Tirzepatide's patent protection makes it the main object of cross-border counterfeiting.

events.event: FDA and CDC tie 200+ emergency visits and four deaths in 19 states to imported and counterfeit GLP-1 product, chiefly mis-concentrated Indian-origin multi-dose vials and endotoxin-contaminated 'research' tirzepatide from Chinese suppliers sold via Telegram, gyms and flea markets; CBP reports seizures at six times the 2026 rate.

FDA adds a class-wide Warnings and Precautions label for NAION to all GLP-1 receptor agonists, including dual and triple agonists, after a Sentinel analysis and two large cohorts find a small, consistent excess risk.

CMS converts the expiring Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot into a multi-year Innovation Center model through 2031, keeping $245/$50 branded pricing and adding a generic-first rule from mid-2028; 41 state Medicaid programmes and DC sign on at federally negotiated rates.

ASAM guideline endorses GLP-1 receptor agonists as an option for alcohol use disorder, the VA adopts it within weeks, and telehealth firms launch branded low-dose 'calm and focus' semaglutide protocols marketed for craving, drawing FTC warning letters over the claims.

Novo Nordisk settles US semaglutide patent litigation with Viatris and two other ANDA filers, licensing generic injection sales years before the 2031–32 patent expiry, and launches an authorised generic at $49/month; cost-plus pharmacies list at $39, and HRSA begins free provision at community health centres on July 1.

Amgen files a BLA for MariTide, the first monthly incretin injection, under a National Priority Voucher with a decision expected early 2029, five months after Lilly's retatrutide was approved at a $1,299 list price.

open_tensions: Public programmes are now the default payer, but Medicaid work requirements and state opt-outs make coverage intermittent for the poorest users. The largest population cycling on and off the drug is cycling by paperwork, and the CMS registry will be the first to measure what that does.

Thinness is free and muscle is bought. Stratification has moved to next-generation drugs, coaching and lean mass, and MariTide's price and coverage in 2029 will decide whether the monthly shot becomes a clinic default or a premium product.
The reward-blunting mechanism is a guideline-endorsed AUD treatment, a marketed lifestyle product and an unquantified side effect at once. FDA has no category for 'calm' and has left it to the FTC.

The NAION class warning was written for people with obesity and diabetes. Benefit–risk for the growing population of non-obese wellness and calm users, and for adolescents facing decades of exposure, has not been calculated by anyone with authority to act on it.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic tirzepatide exists; Zepbound and Mounjaro remain Lilly-only.
Foundayo (orforglipron) remains on the US market, with its starting oral dose still sold at $149/month through TrumpRx and LillyDirect.
Medicare still pays about $245/month for branded GLP-1s with a $50 beneficiary copay for those who qualify.
The FDA's January 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning from Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound labels stands, and the signal remains classed as debunked.
Weight regain on discontinuation remains established, and manufacturers and payers still frame incretins as chronic, indefinite therapy.

prose.headline: Thin Is Free Now. Muscle Costs Extra: Inside the Year Generic Semaglutide Hit $39
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the autumn of 2028 roughly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, and for the first time the drug most of them take is not, strictly, a brand. In June Novo Nordisk settled its patent fight with Viatris and two other generic filers. The deal licenses US sale of generic semaglutide years ahead of the 2031 patent cliff, and Novo launched its own authorised generic at $49 a month. Cost-plus pharmacies list it at $39. The settlement was not generosity. Through 2027 Indian and Chinese product poured in through Telegram channels, gym lockers and flea markets. That May, the FDA and CDC tied more than two hundred emergency visits and four deaths to vials labelled at one concentration and filled at another, and to 'research' tirzepatide carrying bacterial endotoxin. A brand that could be undercut by a twenty-dollar vial from Hyderabad was worth less than a licensed price floor and a quiet tariff understanding.

The payer is now mostly the government. At the end of 2027, Medicare's eighteen-month pilot was rolled into a multi-year federal model. Branded drugs still cost Medicare about $245 a month and beneficiaries $50, but since July new starts are steered to generic semaglutide at no copay. Forty-one state Medicaid programmes cover the drugs. A federal programme hands generic pens free to uninsured adults under 250 percent of the poverty line at community health centres, which matters most in states like Texas that never expanded Medicaid. Employers keep retreating: fewer than half still cover weight management, and many of those cover only the generic. Public programmes now pay for just over half of all fills. The Medicaid work requirements that began in 2027 push people off coverage, and therefore off the drug, and back on again, in rhythms set by paperwork rather than by doctors.

Price has stopped being the gate. Income has not. Lilly's retatrutide, approved in April with a label for skin dysesthesia, produces losses near 28 percent and lists at $1,299; Lilly's direct channel sells it for $699, and almost no plan covers it. Monthly dosing, which would end the weekly negotiation with a pen, is still only a filing: Amgen submitted MariTide in September under a priority voucher, and a decision is expected early next year. Meanwhile the affluent buy what a free pen cannot provide, which is muscle. In Austin and Dallas, DEXA printouts, lean-mass percentages and strength coaches are the visible part of a weight loss that is otherwise free. Among home health aides and warehouse workers in Houston, 'clinic thin' describes a body that has lost weight without gaining shape, and it is not a compliment.

The drug has also moved into bodies without obesity. Low-dose generic semaglutide, sold by telehealth firms as metabolic and longevity care, is ordinary among professionals in middle age. Some of the same firms now sell the blunting directly, with protocols named for quiet and focus, marketed against food noise, scrolling and the second drink, and pitched to Chicago options traders and sales floors. The FTC has sent letters about the claims, but the product is legal. In March the addiction-medicine society endorsed these drugs for alcohol use disorder, which gave the mechanism a respectable name without giving it a label.

The safety picture has shifted in one way that matters. In September 2027 the FDA put an optic-nerve warning on the whole class after its own surveillance found a small but consistent excess of sudden vision loss, and ophthalmologists now ask every patient about the pen. For someone with diabetes and a BMI of forty, the arithmetic still favours the drug. For a thirty-four-year-old taking it to feel calm, nobody has done the arithmetic.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Reyes takes the 2 bus to the health centre on Bissonnet at seven, before her first client. The pen comes in a white paper bag with her name on it and a folded sheet about eyes. Nobody asks for money. Last spring she paid a man at the flea market on Airline forty dollars for a vial and spent a night on the bathroom floor. She doesn't tell the nurse.

Mr. Halvorsen is eighty, retired from Shell, and has a squat rack in his garage in Memorial. His daughter pays for the new one, the Lilly one, and for a trainer named Devon who comes Mondays and Thursdays. Marisol makes him eggs he doesn't finish. He keeps a jar of sour candies by the bed and eats them one at a time, wincing, like medicine.

The daughter arrives at noon in a sleeveless top. She shows her father his scan on her phone, the blue and the red. She looks at Marisol once, kindly, the way you look at a coat in a window.

At the bus stop Marisol reads the sheet. Sudden loss of vision, usually in one eye, often on waking. She closes one eye, then the other, at a billboard across Westheimer: QUIET. Want less. Be more.

Her sister calls from Baton Rouge. Her Medicaid lapsed over the hours form, so she's off it, and the hunger came back in nine days. She asks if Texas would give her one.

At nine Marisol injects in the bathroom. She isn't hungry. She thinks that ought to feel like something.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Retatrutide's BLA was filed Feb 2027 and approved Apr 2028 (14 months after filing)
least_plausible_claims.why: Retatrutide's BLA was planned for ~Q1 2027 with approval expected 2027–28. A 14-month review is fast but arguably plausible only with a priority voucher, and none is cited for it. The candidate also names a voucher for MariTide, so the omission is notable. Magnitude is at the aggressive edge.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Novo Nordisk settles US semaglutide patent litigation with Viatris and two other ANDA filers, licensing generic injection sales years before the 2031–32 patent expiry
least_plausible_claims.why: Novo voluntarily licensing generics roughly three years early, with an authorised generic at $49 (about 96% below list), is a huge unexplained reversal. The stated cause (gray-market undercutting plus a tariff understanding) is thin. Mechanism and magnitude are weak, since the settlement economics for a ~$76B franchise are not shown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Public programmes now pay for ~52% of US incretin fills.
least_plausible_claims.why: Moving from a 2026 baseline of mostly commercial and cash fills (Medicare pilot only starting Jul 2026) to a majority public share in two years requires very fast Medicaid and Medicare uptake. Meanwhile the candidate says Medicaid coverage is interrupted by work-requirement churn, and the Medicare model keeps branded drugs at $245. The figure is asserted rather than derived.

rationale.badness: Net health gains are real (obesity falls to ~33.5%, free generics), but new losers appear: involuntary cycling via Medicaid work requirements, lean-mass loss in older and food-insecure users, and 'clinic thin' class marking. The wellness and 'calm' markets expose non-obese users to NAION and lean-mass risk with no benefit-risk calculation, and reward blunting is marketed with unvalidated 'craving scores'. Epistemic opacity is notable (the FDA has no category for 'calm'; self-reported muted enjoyment in 10–20% of users is unquantified). Overall it is a harder society with new stratification, not a catastrophe.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Nearly every driver is visible in the state and events (generic collapse, public expansion, AUD and wellness, NAION class label, counterfeits, class stratification, HRSA subsidy, marketed 'calm'). The monthly/implant driver is realised only as a filing, with no product on the market, which is a thin honouring. mechanism: Many chains are shown (counterfeit wave → settlement; NAION Sentinel analysis → label; work requirements → cycling), but the Novo settlement and the 52% public share are asserted, and the arithmetic on the cycled share is somewhat convoluted. magnitude: Adoption jumps to 21.3% by stipulation, but the extras are aggressive: 65+ use rising from 9% to 20%, a $49 generic in 2028, retatrutide approved in 14 months, CagriSema approved despite a failed non-inferiority trial, ASAM guidelines within a year of a single small RCT, and 1 in 6 users non-obese. Several of these sit at or beyond the aggressive edge.
rationale.generativity: The prose is rich in scene: Marisol on the Bissonnet bus, Mr. Halvorsen's squat rack and sour candies, the daughter's phone DEXA scan, the QUIET billboard, her sister's Medicaid lapse. The world JSON adds named cities, professions and subcultures (Austin DEXA status, Miami dating apps, AUD recovery meeting splits) that imply many further scenes.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Retatrutide's BLA was filed Feb 2027 and approved Apr 2028 (14 months after filing)
least_plausible_claims.why: The parent said BLA planned ~Q1 2027 with approval 2027–28. A novel triple agonist with a dysesthesia signal and 11.3% AE discontinuation is approved in 14 months, and a postmarketing requirement on ocular outcomes is attached while a class NAION label is already in force. This is aggressive even with priority vouchers.
